Create ONE character or object sprite, rendered entirely as handcrafted paper art: a figure assembled from individually cut pieces of matte colored cardstock and fine-grain craft paper.

STYLE:
Strongly emphasize the physical nature of real paper: visible paper fibers, subtle cardstock grain, crisp cut edges, slightly imperfect hand-cut contours, and tiny natural variations in shape. Use simple, graphic silhouettes and charming handcrafted forms rather than realistic modeling. Each object should be simplified into a small number of flat paper shapes, generally using only one or two solid tones per element. Avoid excessive internal detail.

Create depth primarily through PAPER LAYERING, not through realistic light-and-shadow modeling. Individual paper pieces should sit slightly above or behind neighboring layers, creating narrow, soft, clearly separated cast shadows along their cut edges, like stacked cardstock mounted with tiny spacers. Keep all shapes internally flat and evenly colored. No volumetric shading inside leaves, bean pods, soil, stones, or plants.

CRITICAL STYLE RULE:
Flat paper shapes must remain visibly FLAT.
Do not create volume by shading the interior of a shape.
A leaf, bean pod, cloud, stone, or plant must look like a flat silhouette cut from cardstock, not a miniature three-dimensional object.
Depth may appear ONLY through overlapping separate sheets and the thin cast shadow underneath their cut edges.

Use occasional very shallow debossed or embossed paper details for simple veins, folds, grooves, or decorative lines, but keep these extremely subtle. They should look pressed into paper rather than sculpted.

SUBJECT AND POSE:
This is the classic Christmas poem THE NIGHT BEFORE CHRISTMAS (A Visit from St. Nicholas, Clement C. Moore, 1823), set in a generic early-1800s country house on a snowy Christmas Eve night: candles, wooden shutters, a stone fireplace, stockings, nightcaps. Simple, warm, gentle, kid-friendly bedtime mood. No Disney look, no film or advertisement look, no modern objects (no electric lights, no plastic, no Christmas tree).
The reference image is a DIFFERENT character (the father) shown ONLY for paper style and scale: draw St. Nicholas NOT like him, but with his FACE as wide as the father's head and his whole height only 0.7 of the father's height (small, round and short). ST. NICHOLAS exactly as the 1823 poem describes him (NOT a tall modern Santa, NOT a soft-drink advertisement Santa): a SMALL, chubby, plump, jolly old ELF-LIKE man, only 2 heads tall, with a round little belly. He is dressed ALL IN FUR from his head to his foot: a fur suit, fur trousers and a fur cap in bean red (#A93B32), all fur trims (cap band, cuffs, hem, front edge) in paper cream (#F6ECD8, a sooty cream, not bright white); three or four small ash-grey (#8B8680) soot patches on the sleeves, hem and cap ("tarnished with ashes and soot"); a cocoa (#4E3524) belt with a straw-gold (#D9A94E) buckle; cocoa boots. On his back a big kraft (#C9A574) toy sack tied with a straw-gold string, with the tips of toys peeking out of its mouth (a persimmon #E8703A drum, a straw-gold trumpet, a sky-blue #3E7CB1 ball; NO dolls). NO pipe, NO smoke, NO glasses.
POSE AND EXPRESSION: standing in three-quarter SIDE VIEW FACING LEFT, the toy sack on his back, one hand holding the sack string at his shoulder, the other hand on his round belly. MERRY face: bow-shaped smile, rosy cheeks, twinkling eyes. Looking LEFT.

If a reference image is attached, it shows how this character (or this family of objects) is drawn in this exact style: keep the same drawing style, body shapes, face and proportions; take the COLOURS, clothes, markings and POSE from the SUBJECT text above when it says so.

FRAMING:
Square 1:1 image. The whole figure is visible and centred, filling about 80% of the frame. Background: a completely flat, uniform, solid magenta (#FF00FF) chroma-key sheet with no texture, no floor, no ground shadow, no extra props, no border. Nothing else in the image.

STYLE:
Strongly emphasize the physical nature of real paper: visible paper fibers, subtle cardstock grain, crisp cut edges, slightly imperfect hand-cut contours, and tiny natural variations in shape. Create depth primarily through PAPER LAYERING, not through realistic light-and-shadow modeling. CRITICAL STYLE RULE:

Use occasional very shallow debossed or embossed paper details for simple veins, folds, grooves, or decorative lines, but keep these extremely subtle. They should look pressed into paper rather than sculpted.

Hand-cut layered paper art, handcrafted stop-motion paper diorama aesthetic.

Create ONE character or object sprite, rendered entirely as handcrafted paper art: a figure assembled from individually cut pieces of matte colored cardstock and fine-grain craft paper.

STYLE:
Strongly emphasize the physical nature of real paper: visible paper fibers, subtle cardstock grain, crisp cut edges, slightly imperfect hand-cut contours, and tiny natural variations in shape. Use simple, graphic silhouettes and charming handcrafted forms rather than realistic modeling. Each object should be simplified into a small number of flat paper shapes, generally using only one or two solid tones per element. Avoid excessive internal detail.

Create depth primarily through PAPER LAYERING, not through realistic light-and-shadow modeling. Individual paper pieces should sit slightly above or behind neighboring layers, creating narrow, soft, clearly separated cast shadows along their cut edges, like stacked cardstock mounted with tiny spacers. Keep all shapes internally flat and evenly colored. No volumetric shading inside leaves, bean pods, soil, stones, or plants.

CRITICAL STYLE RULE:
Flat paper shapes must remain visibly FLAT.
Do not create volume by shading the interior of a shape.
A leaf, bean pod, cloud, stone, or plant must look like a flat silhouette cut from cardstock, not a miniature three-dimensional object.
Depth may appear ONLY through overlapping separate sheets and the thin cast shadow underneath their cut edges.

Use occasional very shallow debossed or embossed paper details for simple veins, folds, grooves, or decorative lines, but keep these extremely subtle. They should look pressed into paper rather than sculpted.

Hand-cut layered paper art, handcrafted stop-motion paper diorama aesthetic.

Create ONE character or object sprite, rendered entirely as handcrafted paper art: a figure assembled from individually cut pieces of matte colored cardstock and fine-grain craft paper.

STYLE:
Strongly emphasize the physical nature of real paper: visible paper fibers, subtle cardstock grain, crisp cut edges, slightly imperfect hand-cut contours, and tiny natural variations in shape. Use simple, graphic silhouettes and charming handcrafted forms rather than realistic modeling. Each object should be simplified into a small number of flat paper shapes, generally using only one or two solid tones per element. Avoid excessive internal detail.

Create depth primarily through PAPER LAYERING, not through realistic light-and-shadow modeling. Individual paper pieces should sit slightly above or behind neighboring layers, creating narrow, soft, clearly separated cast shadows along their cut edges, like stacked cardstock mounted with tiny spacers. Keep all shapes internally flat and evenly colored. No volumetric shading inside leaves, bean pods, soil, stones, or plants.

CRITICAL STYLE RULE:
Flat paper shapes must remain visibly FLAT.
Do not create volume by shading the interior of a shape.
A leaf, bean pod, cloud, stone, or plant must look like a flat silhouette cut from cardstock, not a miniature three-dimensional object.
Depth may appear ONLY through overlapping separate sheets and the thin cast shadow underneath their cut edges.

Use occasional very shallow debossed or embossed paper details for simple veins, folds, grooves, or decorative lines, but keep these extremely subtle. They should look pressed into paper rather than sculpted.

Strongly emphasize the physical nature of real paper: visible paper fibers, subtle cardstock grain, crisp cut edges, slightly imperfect hand-cut contours, and tiny natural variations in shape. Use simple, graphic silhouettes and charming handcrafted forms rather than realistic modeling. Each object should be simplified into a small number of flat paper shapes, generally using only one or two solid tones per element. Avoid excessive internal detail.

Create depth primarily through PAPER LAYERING, not through realistic light-and-shadow modeling. Individual paper pieces should sit slightly above or behind neighboring layers, creating narrow, soft, clearly separated cast shadows along their cut edges, like stacked cardstock mounted with tiny spacers. Keep all shapes internally flat and evenly colored. No volumetric shading inside leaves, bean pods, soil, stones, or plants.

CRITICAL STYLE RULE:
Flat paper shapes must remain visibly FLAT.
Do not create volume by shading the interior of a shape.
A leaf, bean pod, cloud, stone, or plant must look like a flat silhouette cut from cardstock, not a miniature three-dimensional object.
Depth may appear ONLY through overlapping separate sheets and the thin cast shadow underneath their cut edges.

Use occasional very shallow debossed or embossed paper details for simple veins, folds, grooves, or decorative lines, but keep these extremely subtle. They should look pressed into paper rather than sculpted.

A landscape 4:3 thumbnail tile, a full-bleed rectangular paper diorama picture (no cream sheet, no window, no border, no frame). Only 2 or 3 flat paper depth planes.
